title: What intervals change in the body
goal: Compare the adaptations to HIIT, SIT and continuous training, central and peripheral, and explain why trained athletes gain less.

steps.title: Intervals and steady training: the same adaptations
steps.text:
Tier 2 gave the headline: HIIT raises VO₂max a little more than [continuous training](g:continuous-training). MacInnis and Gibala's review goes further. Both HIIT and [SIT](g:sprint-interval-training) bring the classic adaptations of moderate continuous training: a higher VO₂max and more [mitochondria](g:mitochondria) [[c:classic-adaptations]].

How they compare depends on what is held equal [[c:volume-compare]]:

- For the **same training volume**, HIIT raises VO₂max more than moderate continuous training.
- SIT and moderate continuous training raise VO₂max about **equally**, even though SIT is far less work.

A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 16 [RCTs](g:rct) agrees on SIT: as effective as moderate continuous training, with less activity [[c:gist-sit]].

claims.text: HIIT and SIT both bring the classic adaptations of moderate continuous training, such as higher VO₂max and mitochondrial content.

evidence.quote: Both forms of interval training induce the classic physiological adaptations characteristic of moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) such as increased aerobic capacity (V̇O2 max ) and mitochondrial content.

claims.text: For a given volume, HIIT raises VO₂max more than moderate continuous training; SIT and moderate continuous training raise it similarly despite different volumes.

evidence.quote: At the whole-body level, V̇O2 max is generally increased more by HIIT than MICT for a given training volume, whereas SIT and MICT similarly improve V̇O2 max despite differences in training volume.

claims.text: Across 16 RCTs, SIT improved aerobic capacity about as much as moderate continuous training, with less volume.

evidence.quote: Relative to continuous endurance training of moderate intensity, SIT presents an equally effective alternative with a reduced volume of activity.

steps.title: Two weeks, a tenth of the work
steps.text:
The landmark test: 16 active young men trained six times in two weeks. The SIT group did 4–6 × 30 s all-out with 4 min recovery; the endurance group rode 90–120 min steady. Training time was about **2.5 h vs 10.5 h**, and work about **630 vs 6500 kJ**: roughly 90% less for SIT [[c:gibala-volume]]. [Time trials](g:time-trial) improved, and muscle oxidative capacity rose, about equally in both groups [[c:gibala-similar]].

Impressive, but read the sample: 8 men per group, not trained, 2 weeks. It shows SIT is a time-efficient way to start adapting. It doesn't show SIT can replace volume for a trained athlete.

claims.text: Over 2 weeks, SIT took about 2.5 h and 630 kJ against about 10.5 h and 6500 kJ for endurance training: about 90% less volume.

evidence.quote: Training time commitment over 2 weeks was approximately 2.5 h for SIT and approximately 10.5 h for ET, and total training volume was approximately 90% lower for SIT versus ET ( approximately 630 versus approximately 6500 kJ).

claims.text: Despite the difference in volume, SIT and endurance training gave similar gains in time-trial performance and muscle oxidative capacity in young active men.

evidence.quote: Given the large difference in training volume, these data demonstrate that SIT is a time-efficient strategy to induce rapid adaptations in skeletal muscle and exercise performance that are comparable to ET in young active men.

steps.title: Heart or muscle?
steps.text:
VO₂max can rise because the heart pumps more blood (central) or because muscles extract and use more O₂ (peripheral). A 2022 meta-analysis of 32 studies, 369 people, sorted the gains by interval type [[c:rosenblat-cp]]:

| measure | HIIT | SIT |
|---|---|---|
| [plasma volume](g:plasma-volume) | up | no clear change |
| heart: maximal [stroke volume](g:stroke-volume) and [cardiac output](g:cardiac-output) | up | no clear change |
| [citrate synthase](g:citrate-synthase) | up | up |
| [capillary density](g:capillary-density), mitochondrial respiration | no clear change | up |

Only HIIT clearly improved the heart; in one 4 × 4 min study, VO₂max rose in step with stroke volume [[c:helgerud-sv]]. SIT's gains were in the muscle. Caution: 49 of 369 were women, and data on capillaries and blood volume are thin [[c:less-evidence]].

claims.text: Only HIIT clearly improved cardiac function and plasma volume; both HIIT and SIT raised citrate synthase, while capillary density and mitochondrial respiration changed only with SIT.

evidence.quote: Only HIIT led to a statistically significant improvement in cardiac function.
There were only statistically significant changes in hematological measures (plasma volume) following HIIT.
Both HIIT and SIT increased maximal citrate synthase activity, while changes in other peripheral measures (capillary density, mitochondrial respiration) only occurred with SIT.

claims.text: After 8 weeks of 4 × 4 min intervals, VO₂max changes matched changes in stroke volume.

evidence.quote: The changes in VO2max correspond with changes in SV, indicating a close link between the two.

claims.text: Evidence on how intensity changes capillary density, maximal stroke volume and cardiac output, and blood volume is limited.

evidence.quote: There is less evidence available regarding the role of exercise intensity in mediating changes in skeletal muscle capillary density, maximum stroke volume and cardiac output, and blood volume.

steps.title: Intensity sets off the muscle signal
steps.text:
Why can a few minutes of hard work match hours of steady work inside the muscle? The cell stress and signals that start [mitochondrial biogenesis](g:mitochondrial-biogenesis) depend largely on intensity. Limited work even suggests HIIT raises mitochondrial content more than moderate continuous training when the work done is matched in the same person [[c:intensity-signal]].

That SIT raises mitochondrial content as much as continuous training, with far less volume, is well established [[c:sit-mito]].

This doesn't make volume useless: the adaptation module showed both levers work. It explains why intervals are so time-efficient.

claims.text: The signals for mitochondrial biogenesis depend largely on intensity; limited work suggests HIIT raises mitochondrial content more than moderate continuous training when work is matched within a person.

evidence.quote: With respect to skeletal muscle adaptations, cellular stress and the resultant metabolic signals for mitochondrial biogenesis depend largely on exercise intensity, with limited work suggesting that increases in mitochondrial content are superior after HIIT compared to MICT, at least when matched-work comparisons are made within the same individual.

claims.text: SIT raises mitochondrial content about as much as moderate continuous training, despite less volume.

evidence.quote: It is well established that SIT increases mitochondrial content to a similar extent to MICT despite a reduced exercise volume.

steps.title: Trained athletes: smaller gains, intervals matter more
steps.text:
[Training status](g:training-status) changes the picture. In highly trained athletes, more easy volume doesn't seem to raise performance or VO₂peak further; an early review concluded that gains then come only from HIIT [[c:laursen-trained]]. In a meta-analysis of 29 studies, interval training improved [time trial](g:time-trial) performance by about **2%** in trained people, against up to **6%** in less trained ones [[c:rosenblat-status]].

Which intervals for trained cyclists? In Rønnestad's trials, 30/15 short intervals beat effort-matched 4–5 min intervals: VO₂max +8.7% vs +2.6% over 10 weeks, and 20-min power +4.7% vs −1.4% in elite riders over 3 weeks [[c:ronn-short]]. But groups were small (7–9 riders), from one lab.

claims.text: In highly trained athletes, extra submaximal volume doesn't seem to improve performance further; an early review concluded gains come only through HIIT.

evidence.quote: an additional increase in submaximal training (i.e. volume) in highly trained individuals does not appear to further enhance either endurance performance or associated physiological variables
It seems that, for athletes who are already trained, improvements in endurance performance can be achieved only through high-intensity interval training (HIT).

claims.text: Interval training improved time-trial performance by about 2% in trained people and by up to about 6% in less trained people.

evidence.quote: Training status played a significant role in improvements in TT performance with trained individuals only seeing improvements of approximately 2% whereas individuals of lower training status demonstrated improvements as high as 6%.

claims.text: In trained and elite cyclists, effort-matched 30/15 short intervals gave larger gains than 4–5 min long intervals.

evidence.quote: The SI group achieved a larger relative improvement in VO(2max) than the LI group (8.7% ± 5.0% vs 2.6% ± 5.2%), respectively, P ≤ 0.05).
Improvements in performance measured as mean power output during 20-minute cycling test were greater (P < .01) in SI compared with LI (4.7 ± 4.4% vs -1.4 ± 2.2%, respectively).

points: HIIT and SIT bring the classic endurance adaptations: higher VO₂max and more mitochondria.
Per unit of volume, HIIT beats moderate continuous training for VO₂max; SIT matches it with about 90% less work, at least in untrained people over short periods.
HIIT shows clearer central gains (plasma volume, heart); SIT's extra gains are mostly in the muscle. Evidence is thin and mostly from men.
Intensity drives the muscle's signal for new mitochondria, which is why intervals are time-efficient.
Trained athletes gain less (about 2% in time trials vs up to 6%); in trained cyclists, 30/15 short intervals beat effort-matched long ones in small trials.

variants.stem: Two groups do the same total work for 8 weeks: one as HIIT, one as moderate continuous training. What does the evidence predict for VO₂max?

options.why: Right: for a given training volume, HIIT generally raises VO₂max more than moderate continuous training.

options.text: A larger rise with continuous training
options.why: For matched volume it is HIIT, not continuous training, that tends to give more.
Both kinds of training raise VO₂max a lot in healthy adults.
Continuous training raises VO₂max too; HIIT just adds a little more.

variants.stem: A recreational runner has only 3 short sessions a week and wants a higher VO₂max. Compared with longer moderate steady runs, what do SIT sessions offer?

options.text: About the same VO₂max gain for far less work
options.why: Right: SIT is about as effective as moderate continuous training for aerobic capacity, with much less volume.

options.text: A much larger VO₂max gain for the same time
options.why: SIT matches, rather than beats, moderate continuous training; HIIT is the type that adds a little more.

options.text: No VO₂max gain, only sprint speed
options.why: SIT does raise VO₂max: by a small-to-moderate effect across 16 RCTs.

options.text: A VO₂max gain only after a year
options.why: SIT gains appear within weeks; Gibala's group saw changes in 2 weeks.

variants.stem: A coach cites Gibala 2006 to replace a trained triathlete's long rides with 3 SIT sessions a week. What is the main problem with that use of the study?

options.text: It tested 16 young active men for only 2 weeks
options.why: Right: 8 young active men per group over 2 weeks says little about long-term gains in a trained athlete.

options.text: It found SIT worse than endurance training
options.why: It found similar gains in both groups, despite about 90% less work with SIT.
It measured time trials of 50 and 750 kJ, and both groups improved.

options.text: SIT can't be done on a bike
options.why: The study's SIT was done on a cycle ergometer.

variants.stem: A cyclist's main weakness is a low maximal cardiac output. According to the 2022 meta-analysis, which interval type has the clearer evidence for central gains?

options.why: Right: only HIIT clearly improved cardiac function and plasma volume.
SIT's gains showed up mostly in the muscle: capillaries and mitochondrial respiration.
HIIT did change central factors: plasma volume, maximal stroke volume and cardiac output.
Central gains were clear only after HIIT.

variants.stem: After 6 weeks of SIT, a runner's VO₂max has risen. Based on the 2022 meta-analysis, where is the gain most likely to come from?

options.why: Right: with SIT, changes in capillary density and mitochondrial respiration were seen, not clear heart changes.

options.text: A bigger heart and more plasma
options.why: Central changes were clear after HIIT, not after SIT.
Maximal heart rate doesn't rise with training; it is not a usual source of VO₂max gains.
Changes in blood were seen only with HIIT, and were in plasma volume.

variants.stem: After 8 weeks of 4 × 4 min running intervals, moderately trained men raised their VO₂max. Which change tracked that rise most closely?

options.why: Right: in Helgerud's study, VO₂max changes corresponded with changes in stroke volume.
Maximal heart rate doesn't rise with training; stroke volume does.
PCr stores matter for sprints, not for VO₂max.

options.text: A lower blood lactate at rest
options.why: Resting lactate is near baseline before and after; it doesn't set VO₂max.

variants.stem: Why can a short SIT session start nearly as much mitochondrial growth as a long steady ride?

options.text: The muscle's signal depends mainly on intensity
options.why: Right: cell stress and the signals for mitochondrial biogenesis depend largely on exercise intensity.

options.text: Sprints burn more total energy than a long ride
options.why: SIT uses far less energy: about 630 vs 6500 kJ over two weeks in Gibala's study.
Steady training also raises mitochondrial content.
Maximal heart rate doesn't rise with training, and it isn't what signals mitochondria.

variants.stem: A well-trained cyclist does 8 weeks of HIIT and improves a 40 km time trial by 2%. Her friend, new to cycling, improved by 6% on a similar plan. What's the best judgement?

options.why: Right: across 29 studies, trained people gained about 2% in time trials, less trained ones up to 6%.

options.text: Her plan failed: 2% is too small to matter
options.why: For a trained athlete 2% is a typical and meaningful gain.

options.text: She should switch to more easy volume instead
options.why: In highly trained athletes, extra easy volume doesn't seem to raise performance further.

options.text: The friend must have trained more
options.why: Larger gains in less trained people are expected even with the same plan.

variants.stem: A trained cyclist does two interval sessions a week and wants the best gain in VO₂max and 20-min power. Based on Rønnestad's trials, which format is the better bet?

options.why: Right: effort-matched 30/15 short intervals gave larger gains than 4–5 min intervals in trained and elite cyclists, in small trials.
This was the comparison format; it gave smaller gains in those trials.
SIT wasn't tested in these trials; it targets the muscle more than the heart.
Extra easy volume seems to add little for already trained athletes.
